newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU assessment of nations not ready for membership.
newsitem.headline: EU assessment of nations not ready for membership.

text.p: Following are the main reasons given by the European Commission on Wednesday for recommending that Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Lithuania and Latvia are not yet ready for European Union entry talks.
The EU executive argues that that they would be unable to cope with the demands of market reforms or they do not yet display enough political openness, especially in the case of Slovakia.
ROMANIA
Romania wins praise for its political reform efforts following the arrival of a new government, but the Commission says that has not translated into economic growth.

With a population of 22.6 million and a GDP per head that is 24 percent of the EU's average, Romania has undertaken a radical programme of economic reform while showing a worsening trade and budget deficit along with rising inflation.

Romania would face serious difficulties coping with competitive pressure in the EU in the medium term, the Commission says, since much of its industry is obsolete and its agriculture sector needs to be modernised.

The country also needs to improve respect for fundamental rights, for example by fighting corruption, improving the judicial system and protecting individuals from the police and secret services, it says.
BULGARIA

Following the arrival of a new government, Bulgaria is on its way to satisfying the political criteria for EU membership, but its economic progress has been limited by the absence of a commitment to market-oriented policies, the Commission says.

While democratic institutions are stable, Bulgaria needs to make considerable effort to fight against corruption, improve the judicial system and protect citizens from abuses by the police and secret services, it says.

Bulgaria, with 8.3 million people and a GDP per capita at 24 percent of the EU average, has just begun making structural changes to its economy after six "largely wasted years", the Commissions says. It has been hampered by incomplete land reform, slow privatisation and economic instability.
SLOVAKIA
Despite outwardly showing signs of being ready for EU membership, Slovakia displays some worrying faults -- particularly with regard to human rights, the Commission says.
With 5.4 million people and a GDP per capita of 41 percent of the EU average, Slovakia should be able to cope with the competitive pressures in the EU in the medium term, it says.
The country has introduced most of the reforms needed to establish a market economy.

But on political criteria, the Commission is damning, saying the government does not sufficiently respect the powers devolved by the constitution to other bodies and too often disregards the rights of the opposition. The use by the government of the police and secret services is also worrying, it adds.
LITHUANIA

Lithuania has stable democratic institutions and has made considerable progress in creating a market economy, but it would have serious problems coping with competitive pressures in the EU in the medium term, the Commission says.
With a population of 3.7 million and a GDP per head that is 24 percent of the EU average, Lithuania has largely liberalised trade and prices and made progress in stabilising its economy, it says.

However, it still needs to advance in areas including relative price adjustments, large-scale privatisation and bankruptcy proceedings, it adds. The country also needs to restructure its industry, modernise its agriculture sector and strengthen its banking system, while also enforcing financial discipline for companies.
LATVIA

Latvia has good democratic institutions and has made considerable progress in creating a market economy, but would have serious difficulties coping with competitive pressures within the EU in the medium term, the Commission says.
In the political area, it also needs to boost the rate of naturalisation of Russian-speaking non-citizens, it says.

Latvia, with a population of 2.5 million and a GDP per head at only 18 percent of the EU average, has made headway in stabilising its economy. However, effective implementation of legislation lags, the needed regulatory bodies are not all in place and privatisation is incomplete, the Commission says.
The country also needs to restructure its industry, modernise its agriculture sector and strengthen its banking sector, it says.
